To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) any object can form the basis of an interesting and engaging story and act as an entry point to a network of meaning; (2) these networks of meaning are at risk of being lost as time goes on; and (3) the design of augmented memory systems should be informed by the different types of discourse inherent in these object memories.

we found that the use of an augmented memory technology such as the Tales of Things tagging system, in a context where people are invited to share stories about everyday things that have a special meaning for them, can stimulate rich conversations about memories that are linked to these things, and that the design of such systems can be informed by these conversations.

the design of augmented memory systems should: (1) be based on the idea of a network of meaning; (2) allow the user to decide what to share and with whom; (3) be designed in such a way that the system is able to cope with the diversity of objects and their meaning networks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how to augment objects with memories, and how to design for the sharing and socialisation of memories in the context of the Internet of Old Things.
the design of systems that enable people to capture, share, and access their personal and social memories.
the question of what it means to make memories and meaning networks of things accessible and shareable and what the implications are for the design of systems that support this.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Internet of Things is an augmented memory system, but not necessarily one that is designed for that specific purpose.

the design of augmented memory systems needs to take the different types of object stories and their inherent networks of meaning into account and that such systems should be designed in such a way as to support the creation of meaningful connections between people and objects.

the design of augmented memory systems should be driven by an understanding of the different discourses inherent in object stories and should aim at supporting the sharing of these stories in the context of a networked and social memory system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the design of augmented memory systems is not only a technical endeavour but also requires a thorough understanding of how we relate to our objects, the stories they tell and the memories they evoke.
the Internet of Things can be used as a means of augmenting everyday things with personal and social meaning.

the Internet of Things is not only about things but also about the memories, stories and networks of meaning associated with these things and that the Internet of things should therefore be considered as an Internet of memories.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Internet of Things has the potential to be much more than just an Internet of Things, but also an Internet of Old Things and an Internet of Stories.
the augmentation of things with stories is a promising way to support the preservation of personal and social memories.
the Internet of Things has to be seen as a system that is not only concerned with the augmentation of objects but also with the augmentation of memory and meaning.
